concept: 91.169 is the regulation that decides whether an IFR flight plan must list an alternate airport
q: Which regulation tells you whether your IFR flight plan needs an alternate, and what is it called?
a: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.' In plain English it says every IFR flight plan must name an alternate airport unless the destination passes a two-part test: the destination has a published instrument approach, and the forecast weather there meets the 1-2-3 rule. Fail either part and you must file an alternate.
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: First gate of the flowchart: destination must have at least one published instrument approach available
q: What is the first question in the alternate decision tree?
a: Whether the destination has at least one published instrument approach procedure. If it has none, no amount of good forecast weather helps; 91.169 requires an alternate automatically. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.' Only when the destination has an approach do you go on to test the forecast against the 1-2-3 rule.
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: The two gates are joined by AND: approach available AND 1-2-3 weather met
q: Are the instrument approach test and the 1-2-3 weather test joined by AND or by OR?
a: By AND. You skip the alternate only if the destination has a published instrument approach and the forecast meets 1-2-3. The flowchart puts both conditions inside one box joined by AND for exactly that reason. Fail either one and the answer is alternate required. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: 1-2-3 rule time window: 1 hour before ETA through 1 hour after ETA
q: Over what time window must the destination forecast be checked for the 1-2-3 rule?
a: From 1 hour before through 1 hour after your ETA, a two hour window centered on your estimated time of arrival. The forecast must hold the required ceiling and visibility for that whole window, so a TEMPO or PROB group that dips below minimums anywhere inside it forces an alternate. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: 1-2-3 rule ceiling: 2,000 ft ceilings or higher
q: What ceiling must the destination be forecast to have to avoid filing an alternate?
a: At least 2,000 feet. The forecast ceiling must be 2,000 feet or higher throughout the window running from one hour before to one hour after ETA. This is the 2 of the 1-2-3 rule. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: 1-2-3 rule visibility: 3 SM visibility or greater
q: What visibility must the destination be forecast to have to avoid filing an alternate?
a: At least 3 statute miles, forecast throughout the window from one hour before to one hour after ETA. This is the 3 of the 1-2-3 rule. Note the unit carefully: statute miles, not nautical miles. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: Flowchart branch: No to either gate means an alternate is required
q: The destination fails the 1-2-3 test. What does the flowchart tell you to do?
a: File an alternate. A no at the first box sends you down the alternate required path, where you pick a candidate airport and test it against the alternate minimums. Filing an alternate also drives fuel planning: Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.167, 'Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions,' requires enough fuel to reach the destination, then the alternate, then fly 45 minutes at normal cruise.
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: Flowchart branch: Yes to both gates means no alternate required
q: The destination passes both tests. Must you still file an alternate?
a: No, no alternate is required. With a published approach and a forecast of 2,000 foot ceilings and 3 statute miles from one hour before to one hour after ETA, 91.169 lets you leave the alternate block blank. Many pilots still file one, because the rule is a legal floor and not a judgment; in a Warrior II with no ice protection and modest range, a named alternate is cheap insurance.
dup: What is the 1-2-3 rule for filing an alternate, and where does it come from?

concept: Second node: does the chosen alternate have non-standard alternate requirements that can be complied with
q: Once you know an alternate is required, what is the next decision in the chart?
a: Whether your chosen alternate has non-standard alternate minimums and whether you can actually meet them. Some airports carry higher than standard alternate ceilings and visibilities, or are not authorized as an alternate at all, because of terrain, a missing weather reporting source, or an out of service monitoring facility. Check the alternate minimums section of the Terminal Procedures Publication before applying the standard 600-2 or 800-2 numbers.

concept: Branch: non-standard requirements cannot be complied with, so choose a different alternate
q: Your chosen alternate has non-standard minimums you cannot meet. What does the chart say?
a: Choose a different alternate. The flowchart loops you back: you may not file an airport whose published alternate minimums you cannot meet, and you may not file one annotated alternate NA at all. Pick another airport and run it through the same test, again checking its alternate minimums listing before applying the standard numbers.

concept: Third node: are forecast weather minimum requirements met at the alternate at your ETA
q: At what time must the alternate's forecast weather meet the alternate minimums?
a: At your ETA at the alternate, a single point in time, not the two hour window used for the destination. That is one of the most common trip-ups: the destination gets one hour before through one hour after ETA, while the alternate only has to be forecast at the estimated time of arrival. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
dup: When the forecast makes an alternate necessary, what weather must the alternate itself be forecast to have?

concept: Alternate minimums for a precision approach: 600 ft ceiling, 2 SM visibility
q: What are the standard alternate minimums for an airport with a precision approach?
a: 600 foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility, forecast at your ETA. Precision here means an ILS or PAR, and the FAA also allows an approach with vertical guidance such as an LPV to be used for this purpose. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.' These are the standard numbers; always check the alternate minimums page in case the airport is non-standard.
dup: When the forecast makes an alternate necessary, what weather must the alternate itself be forecast to have?

concept: Alternate minimums for a non-precision approach: 800 ft ceiling, 2 SM visibility
q: What are the standard alternate minimums for an airport with only a non-precision approach?
a: 800 foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility, forecast at your ETA. Non-precision means lateral guidance only, such as a VOR, localizer, NDB, or an LNAV only RNAV approach. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.' The visibility is 2 statute miles in both cases; only the ceiling changes, from 600 feet to 800 feet.
dup: When the forecast makes an alternate necessary, what weather must the alternate itself be forecast to have?

concept: Alternate with no instrument approach: must be able to descend from the MEA and land VFR
q: Can you file an airport with no instrument approach as your alternate?
a: Yes, but only if the forecast ceiling and visibility at your ETA will let you descend from the MEA, approach and land under basic VFR. You must be able to leave the airway structure visually and complete the landing with no approach procedure to help you. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.169, 'IFR flight plan: Information required.'
dup: When the forecast makes an alternate necessary, what weather must the alternate itself be forecast to have?

concept: Branch: alternate forecast minimums not met, so choose a different alternate
q: The alternate's forecast at your ETA is below 600-2. What does the flowchart say?
a: Go back and choose a different alternate. The loop in the chart returns you to the same place as a non-standard minimums failure. An airport you cannot legally file does not become filable by hoping the forecast improves; find another one, or delay or cancel the flight if nothing in range qualifies.

concept: WAAS branch node: is your airplane equipped with a WAAS GPS
q: Which equipment question decides how you may use RNAV-only airports in alternate planning?
a: Whether the airplane is equipped with a WAAS GPS, a navigator using the Wide Area Augmentation System and certified to TSO-C145 or TSO-C146. WAAS corrects satellite and ionospheric errors and adds an integrity guarantee, which is why it changes what you may plan on. A 1981 Warrior II has it only if it has been retrofitted; check the equipment list and the avionics actually installed in your panel.
dup: What does WAAS add to GPS?

concept: Non-WAAS outcome: RNAV-only approaches at EITHER destination OR alternate, but not both
q: Without WAAS, how may you plan RNAV-only airports as destination and alternate?
a: You may plan on an airport served only by RNAV approaches at either the destination or the alternate, but not both. One of the two must have a non-RNAV approach you can fly. The restriction exists because a single GPS failure in a non-WAAS airplane would strip you of the approach at both ends of the flight. If your Warrior has a non-WAAS IFR GPS, this is the limitation that applies to you.

concept: WAAS outcome: RNAV-only approaches at BOTH destination AND alternate
q: With a WAAS GPS, how may you plan RNAV-only airports as destination and alternate?
a: You may plan on airports served only by RNAV approaches at both the destination and the alternate. WAAS integrity monitoring removes the single failure concern that restricts non-WAAS aircraft. When you compute the alternate weather requirement, however, the AIM directs you to use the LNAV or circling minimums line, not the LPV line.

concept: The inverted triangle containing the letter A on an approach chart marks non-standard alternate minimums
q: What does a black triangle containing a white letter A on an approach chart tell you?
a: That the airport has non-standard alternate minimums, so the standard 600-2 and 800-2 do not apply and you must look the airport up in the alternate minimums section of the Terminal Procedures Publication. If the symbol carries NA beside it, the airport may not be used as an alternate at all. Its companion, a black triangle containing a white T, marks non-standard takeoff minimums or a departure procedure.

concept: Airspeed indicator white arc: flap operating range, starts at VSO and ends at VFE
q: What does the white arc on the airspeed indicator mark, and where does it begin and end?
a: The flap operating range. It begins at VSO, the stall speed in the landing configuration at maximum gross weight, and ends at VFE, the maximum flap extended speed. Inside the white arc you may select and fly with any approved flap setting. The exact numbers for your 1981 Warrior II are on the face of the instrument and in Section 2 of the POH; confirm them there.
dup: What does the white arc on the airspeed indicator represent?

concept: Airspeed indicator green arc: normal operating range, starts at VS1 and ends at VNO
q: What does the green arc mark on the airspeed indicator, and what are its limits?
a: The normal operating range. It begins at VS1, the stall speed in a specified configuration, conventionally clean with flaps up, and ends at VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed. This is the band you fly in day to day, in smooth or rough air alike. Read the boundaries off your Warrior II's indicator and confirm them against Section 2 of the POH.
dup: What does the green arc on the airspeed indicator represent?

concept: Airspeed indicator yellow arc: caution range, smooth air only, related to maneuvering speed
q: What does the yellow arc mean, and between which two speeds does it run?
a: The caution range: fly there only in smooth air, and with caution. It runs from VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed, up to VNE, the never exceed speed. Above VNO a sharp vertical gust or an abrupt control input can drive the airplane past its design limit load factor. Remember that the caution range sits well above VA, so full control deflection up there can overstress the airframe.
dup: What is Vno and what does the yellow arc mean?

concept: Airspeed indicator red line: warning range, VNE, structural damage possible
q: What does the red line on the airspeed indicator represent?
a: VNE, the never exceed speed, and the start of the warning range. Exceeding it risks structural damage or control surface flutter, and the airplane is not certificated to be flown there under any circumstance. It is a single radial red line at the top of the yellow arc. The Warrior II's VNE is on the dial and in Section 2 of the POH; confirm it there.
dup: What is Vne and how is it marked?

concept: Reading the airspeed indicator dial: which V-speeds the arc boundaries give you and which they do not
q: Which V-speeds can you read directly off the airspeed indicator face, and which cannot?
a: The arc boundaries give you five: VSO, VS1, VFE, VNO and VNE, which are the bottom and top of the white arc, the bottom and top of the green arc, and the red line. VA, VX, VY, VG, VLE and VREF are not marked, because VA and VG change with weight and the climb speeds change with altitude. Those come from the POH or a cockpit placard. On the Warrior II, read the arcs off the dial and confirm against Section 2.
dup: Which V-speeds are marked on the airspeed indicator and which are not?

concept: V-speed: VA, design maneuvering speed
q: What is VA?
a: Design maneuvering speed, the highest speed at which full, abrupt deflection of a single flight control will stall the wing before the structure is overstressed. It is not marked on the airspeed indicator, and it falls as weight falls, because a lighter airplane reaches the limit load factor at a lower speed. Your Warrior II's VA at gross weight and its reduction at lighter weights are published in the POH; use those figures.
dup: What is Va, design maneuvering speed?

concept: V-speed: VS, stall speed in the clean configuration
q: What is VS?
a: The stall speed in the clean configuration, gear up if retractable and flaps up, or more formally the stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed at which the airplane remains controllable. In a fixed gear airplane like the Warrior II it is effectively the flaps up stall. Take the number from Section 2 of the POH; remember it rises with weight, with bank angle and with any load factor above one G.
dup: What is Vs1 and how does it differ from Vso?

concept: V-speed: VSO, stall speed in the landing configuration
q: What is VSO?
a: The stall speed in the landing configuration, meaning full flaps, gear down if retractable and power off, at maximum gross weight. It is the lower end of the white arc, and it anchors approach speed calculations, which conventionally run around 1.3 times VSO. Read your Warrior II's VSO from the bottom of the white arc and confirm it in Section 2 of the POH.
dup: What is Vso and where do you find the number for your aircraft?

concept: V-speed: VS1, stall speed in a specific configuration
q: What is VS1, and how is it different from VSO?
a: VS1 is the stall speed in a specified configuration, conventionally the clean configuration, while VSO is the stall speed in the landing configuration. VS1 is the higher of the two, because without flaps the wing makes less lift at a given speed. VS1 marks the bottom of the green arc and VSO the bottom of the white arc. Both numbers for your Warrior II come from Section 2 of the POH.
dup: What is Vs1 and how does it differ from Vso?

concept: V-speed: VF, design flap speed
q: What is VF, and how does it differ from VFE?
a: VF is the design flap speed, a certification speed the manufacturer uses when stressing the flap structure during design. VFE is the operating limit shown to the pilot: the maximum flap extended speed, marked as the top of the white arc. You fly to VFE; VF sits behind it in the certification basis and is not a cockpit number. Take VFE from your Warrior II's indicator and POH rather than guessing either one.

concept: V-speed: VLE, maximum landing gear extended speed
q: What is VLE, and does it apply to your airplane?
a: Maximum landing gear extended speed, the highest speed at which the airplane may be flown with the gear down and locked. It does not apply to a 1981 Warrior II, which has fixed gear, so no gear limit speed is published for it. Its companion is VLO, maximum landing gear operating speed, the limit for moving the gear in transit. Know both for the oral even though your airplane has neither.
dup: What are Vle and Vlo?

concept: V-speed: VFE, maximum flap extended speed
q: What is VFE and where is it marked?
a: Maximum flap extended speed, the highest speed at which flaps may be extended and the highest speed at which you may fly with them out. It is the top of the white arc. Exceeding it risks bending the flaps or their tracks. The Warrior II has several flap positions, so check whether your POH publishes one VFE or separate limits for each setting, and use the published figures.
dup: What is Vfe and what marks it on the airspeed indicator?

concept: V-speed: VNO, maximum structural cruising speed
q: What is VNO?
a: Maximum structural cruising speed, the top of the green arc and the bottom of the yellow arc. Below it the airplane can absorb a strong vertical gust without exceeding its limit load factor; above it, smooth air only. It is the speed you plan normal cruise around. Read it off the green to yellow boundary on your Warrior II's indicator and confirm it in Section 2 of the POH.
dup: What is Vno and what does the yellow arc mean?

concept: V-speed: VNE, never exceed speed
q: What is VNE?
a: Never exceed speed, the absolute airspeed limit, marked by the red line. Beyond it the airplane may suffer structural failure or control surface flutter, and no condition permits exceeding it. If you find yourself accelerating toward it in a spiral in your Warrior II, reduce power and level the wings before you pull. The number is on the dial and in Section 2 of the POH.
dup: What is Vne and how is it marked?

concept: V-speed: VX, best angle of climb
q: What is VX?
a: Best angle of climb speed, the speed that gives the most altitude gained per unit of horizontal distance. You use it to clear an obstacle off the departure end of the runway. It is slower than VY, and it is not marked on the airspeed indicator. Your Warrior II's VX is in the POH and may be shown as a single figure or as a function of weight; use the published value, not a remembered one.
dup: What is Vx and what does it buy you?

concept: V-speed: VY, best rate of climb
q: What is VY?
a: Best rate of climb speed, the speed that gives the most altitude gained per unit of time. It is the normal climb speed once the obstacles are behind you, and it gets you to cruise altitude soonest. VY is faster than VX at sea level, and the two converge with altitude, meeting at the absolute ceiling. Take your Warrior II's VY from the POH.
dup: What is Vy and when do you use it?

concept: V-speed: VG, best glide speed
q: What is VG?
a: Best glide speed, the speed giving the greatest distance per foot of altitude lost, which is the speed for the best lift to drag ratio. It is the first number you pitch for after an engine failure. It decreases as weight decreases, so a lightly loaded Warrior II glides farthest a few knots below the book figure at gross weight. The published value is in the POH emergency procedures section; use it.
dup: What is best glide speed and how does it change with weight?

concept: V-speed: VREF, calculated final approach speed
q: What is VREF?
a: The calculated final approach speed, the reference speed flown across the threshold, conventionally about 1.3 times VSO at the actual landing weight. Transport and turbine aircraft publish a VREF table that varies with weight. A light trainer like the 1981 Warrior II generally does not; its POH gives normal and short field approach speeds instead. Use the POH approach speeds and apply the handbook's gust correction.

concept: Type of speed: indicated airspeed (IAS)
q: What is indicated airspeed?
a: The speed shown on the face of the airspeed indicator, derived from the difference between pitot ram pressure and static pressure, with no corrections applied. It is uncorrected for instrument error, position error, compressibility and non-standard air. It is also the speed in which every limit and arc on the airplane is expressed, which is why you fly the airplane by indicated airspeed.
dup: What is indicated airspeed and what is calibrated airspeed?

concept: Type of speed: calibrated airspeed (CAS), IAS corrected for instrument and position error
q: What is calibrated airspeed?
a: Indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error. Position error comes from where the static port sits on the airframe and changes with angle of attack, so the correction is largest at low speed and high angle of attack. Your Warrior II's POH carries an airspeed calibration table; that table is what converts an indicated reading into calibrated airspeed.
dup: What is indicated airspeed and what is calibrated airspeed?

concept: Type of speed: equivalent airspeed (EAS), CAS corrected for compressibility error
q: What is equivalent airspeed?
a: Calibrated airspeed corrected for compressibility error. Air behaves as effectively incompressible at low speeds, so below roughly 200 knots and 10,000 feet, equivalent and calibrated airspeed are the same number and a Warrior II pilot never sees a difference. The correction matters to high speed and high altitude aircraft. EAS is the formal step between calibrated and true airspeed.

concept: Type of speed: true airspeed (TAS), EAS corrected for non-standard temperature and pressure
q: What is true airspeed?
a: The actual speed of the airplane through the air mass, which is equivalent airspeed corrected for non-standard temperature and pressure, that is, for air density. Because air thins with altitude, true airspeed exceeds indicated by roughly 2 percent per thousand feet. You plan and compute fuel burn with true airspeed, but you fly the airplane on indicated. Read it from the Warrior II cruise performance tables or a flight computer.
dup: What is true airspeed and how does it relate to indicated airspeed as you climb?

concept: Type of speed: Mach number, the ratio of TAS to the local speed of sound
q: What is Mach number?
a: The ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound. Mach 0.5 means half the local speed of sound. The local speed of sound falls as temperature falls, so the same true airspeed produces a higher Mach number in cold air at altitude. It matters to a Warrior pilot mainly as knowledge test material and to understand why the jets above you fly a Mach number rather than an airspeed.
dup: What is Mach number and why would a piston pilot care about it?

concept: Type of speed: groundspeed, TAS corrected for wind
q: What is groundspeed?
a: The actual speed of the airplane across the ground, which is true airspeed corrected for wind. A headwind subtracts from true airspeed, a tailwind adds to it, and the crosswind component is resolved out in the wind triangle. Groundspeed sets your time en route and therefore your fuel reserve, so it is the number you check against the flight log at every checkpoint.
dup: What is groundspeed and how is it derived?

concept: Type of speed: critical Mach, lowest Mach number at which airflow over any part of the aircraft reaches the speed of sound
q: What is critical Mach number?
a: The lowest Mach number at which airflow over any part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound. The airplane as a whole is still subsonic, but a local region over the thickest part of the wing has gone sonic. Above it a shock wave forms, bringing buffet, a pitch change and loss of control effectiveness. It is a jet and high performance concern rather than a Warrior one, but it is examinable.

concept: Maximum airspeed above 10,000 ft MSL, and the Mach 1 limit
q: Is there an indicated airspeed limit above 10,000 feet MSL?
a: No. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.117, 'Aircraft speed,' sets no indicated airspeed limit above 10,000 feet MSL; the 250 knot restriction stops there. The practical ceiling is Mach 1, because 91.817 prohibits a civil aircraft from operating at a true flight Mach number greater than 1 over the United States. A normally aspirated Warrior II will never approach either figure.
dup: Is there a speed limit above 10,000 feet MSL?

concept: Maximum airspeed below 10,000 ft MSL: 250 knots
q: What is the maximum indicated airspeed below 10,000 feet MSL?
a: 250 knots indicated. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.117, 'Aircraft speed,' says no person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots. Note that it is MSL and not AGL, and that it applies in all airspace at those altitudes. If the minimum safe airspeed for an operation is higher, you may fly that speed and must advise ATC.
dup: What is the maximum indicated airspeed below 10,000 feet MSL?

concept: Maximum airspeed 200 knots under Class B airspace or in a VFR corridor through Class B
q: What is the speed limit beneath a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor through Class B?
a: 200 knots indicated. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.117, 'Aircraft speed,' limits you to 200 knots in the airspace underlying Class B and in any VFR corridor through it. Inside Class B itself the limit reverts to the general 250 knots below 10,000 feet MSL, because the tighter number is aimed at the unseparated traffic squeezed outside and below the shelf.
dup: What is the speed limit beneath a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor through Class B?

concept: Maximum airspeed 200 knots at or below 2,500 ft within 4 NM of a Class C or D airport
q: What is the speed limit at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport?
a: 200 knots indicated. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.117, 'Aircraft speed.' Both conditions must apply together: at or below 2,500 feet above the surface and within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport. The restriction does not apply inside Class B airspace, where 250 knots governs. Note this one is measured in nautical miles and AGL, unlike the 250 knot rule.
dup: What is the speed limit at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport?

concept: Type of altitude: indicated altitude
q: What is indicated altitude?
a: The uncorrected altitude read off the altimeter when the barometric scale is set to the current local altimeter setting. It is what you fly and what you report to ATC, and it is only as accurate as the number in the Kollsman window. That is why you reset it from a station within 100 nautical miles, and why flying into a falling pressure area without a new setting puts you lower than the altimeter claims.
dup: What is indicated altitude and what makes it accurate?

concept: Type of altitude: pressure altitude, altitude corrected for non-standard pressure
q: What is pressure altitude?
a: Altitude corrected for non-standard pressure, that is, the height above the standard datum plane, read by setting the altimeter to 29.92 inches of mercury. It is what you enter into performance charts and the basis for flight levels. You can also compute it: add 1,000 feet for each inch the altimeter setting is below 29.92, and subtract 1,000 feet for each inch above.
dup: What is pressure altitude?

concept: Type of altitude: density altitude, pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature
q: What is density altitude?
a: Pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature, the altitude the airplane behaves as though it were flying at. High, hot and humid conditions raise it; your takeoff roll lengthens, your climb gradient shallows, and your true airspeed for a given indicated reading rises. It is the single number that explains why your Warrior II performs so poorly on a hot afternoon at a high elevation field.
dup: What is density altitude?

concept: Type of altitude: true altitude, altitude above mean sea level
q: What is true altitude?
a: The actual height above mean sea level. Airport elevations, terrain and obstacle heights on charts are all true altitudes. Indicated altitude equals true altitude only in standard conditions; in air colder than standard your true altitude is lower than indicated, which is the reason for cold temperature altitude corrections on instrument approaches.
dup: What is true altitude?

concept: Type of altitude: absolute altitude, altitude above ground level
q: What is absolute altitude?
a: Height above ground level, the vertical distance between the airplane and the terrain directly beneath it. A radar altimeter reads absolute altitude directly; a Warrior II has none, so you derive it by subtracting the charted terrain elevation from your indicated altitude. Obstruction heights and traffic pattern altitudes are commonly expressed this way, labeled AGL.
dup: What is absolute altitude?

concept: Instrument currency lookback period: the preceding 6 calendar months
q: Within what period must the instrument experience requirements have been met to act as PIC under IFR?
a: The preceding 6 calendar months. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c), 'Recent flight experience: Pilot in command,' requires the tasks to be performed and logged within that window, in actual or simulated instrument conditions. Calendar months means you have until the last day of the sixth month, not a rolling date from the day you flew.
dup: What must you have done in the preceding 6 calendar months to act as PIC under IFR?

concept: Instrument currency task: six instrument approaches
q: How many instrument approaches are required for instrument currency, and in what conditions?
a: Six instrument approaches, flown and logged in actual instrument conditions, under a view limiting device in simulated conditions, or in an approved full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c). The regulation does not require them to be of different types or at different airports, though flying a mix is far better practice.
dup: What must you have done in the preceding 6 calendar months to act as PIC under IFR?

concept: Instrument currency task: intercepting and tracking courses using navigation systems
q: Besides approaches and holds, what third task does instrument currency require?
a: Intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c), 'Recent flight experience: Pilot in command.' The regulation does not count or quantify them; you simply have to have done them inside the six month window. Flying the six approaches normally satisfies this by itself, but log it deliberately so the record shows it.
dup: What must you have done in the preceding 6 calendar months to act as PIC under IFR?

concept: Instrument currency task: holding procedures
q: What does instrument currency require regarding holding?
a: Holding procedures and tasks. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c), 'Recent flight experience: Pilot in command.' The requirement covers the entry, flying the pattern, and timing or distance as appropriate. Like course tracking it must be accomplished in actual or simulated instrument conditions, or in an approved device, within the preceding six calendar months.
dup: What must you have done in the preceding 6 calendar months to act as PIC under IFR?

concept: The FAA does not specify how many holds are required, only more than one
q: How many holding patterns does 61.57(c) require you to fly?
a: The regulation does not say. It uses the plural, holding procedures and tasks, and gives no number, unlike the six approaches which are counted exactly. The conservative reading, and the one this guide takes, is more than one. Fly at least two entries from different directions inside the six month window and log them, and no examiner can argue with your record.

concept: Instrument currency tasks may be done in an approved FFS, FTD or ATD without an instructor
q: May the instrument currency tasks be accomplished in a simulator or training device?
a: Yes. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c) permits them in an approved full flight simulator, flight training device, or aviation training device representing the category of aircraft for the instrument rating privileges sought, with the tasks performed in simulated instrument conditions. No flight instructor is required to be present. Note the current rule keys to category of aircraft, not to make and model.
dup: Can instrument currency be regained in a simulator or training device?

concept: The 6 HITS mnemonic for the IFR recency requirements
q: What mnemonic covers the IFR recency requirements, and what does each letter stand for?
a: 6 HITS: 6 instrument approaches; H for holding procedures; I for intercepted a course; T for tracked a course; S for using navigational systems. The I, T and S run together as a single regulatory item, intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems, so the mnemonic expands three letters out of one requirement. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c).

concept: The currency ladder: 6 months current, an additional 6 months to self-regain, then IPC required
q: Describe the three stages of instrument currency after your last qualifying experience.
a: For 6 calendar months you are current and may act as pilot in command under IFR. For the next 6 calendar months you are not current but may regain currency yourself, with a safety pilot, an instructor, or an approved device. Once those 12 calendar months have passed, the only way back is an instrument proficiency check. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c) and 61.57(d).
dup: What happens if you let your instrument currency lapse?

concept: During the additional 6 months, the three tasks may be done with a safety pilot in simulated conditions, or with a CFI or examiner
q: During the additional six month grace period, how may you regain instrument currency?
a: By flying the 6 HITS tasks with a safety pilot in simulated instrument conditions, or with a CFI or examiner aboard, or in an approved simulator or training device. What you may not do is file and fly in actual IFR to accomplish them, because you are not current and cannot act as pilot in command under IFR. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(c).
dup: During the 6-month instrument grace period, what may you do and what may you not do?

concept: After the additional 6 months have passed, an IPC is required
q: You last met the instrument experience requirements 14 months ago. What must you do?
a: Pass an instrument proficiency check. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(d), 'Instrument proficiency check,' applies once more than six calendar months have gone by beyond the six month currency window, that is, after twelve calendar months in total. At that point there is no way to self-regain currency with a safety pilot or a device.
dup: When is an instrument proficiency check required, and what does it involve?

concept: Safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate, which does not have to be current
q: What certificate must a safety pilot hold, and must it be current?
a: At least a private pilot certificate. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.109, 'Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests.' The certificate itself never expires, and a lapsed flight review does not stop someone serving as safety pilot so long as they are not acting as pilot in command. If they are the acting PIC, they must be fully current, including the flight review.
dup: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?

concept: Safety pilot must be rated in the same category and class aircraft
q: What ratings must a safety pilot hold?
a: Category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft being flown. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.109. For your Warrior II that means airplane single-engine land. A type rating is needed only if the aircraft itself requires one. An instrument rating is not required of a safety pilot, because the job is to look outside for traffic, not to fly the approach.
dup: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?

concept: Safety pilot must have a current medical certificate
q: Must a safety pilot hold a medical certificate?
a: Yes. A safety pilot is a required crewmember, so at minimum a current third class medical certificate is required, or BasicMed where the safety pilot is the acting pilot in command and the BasicMed conditions are satisfied. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.109, read with Part 61, Subpart A, 61.3. Without a valid medical, that person cannot legally occupy the seat as your safety pilot.
dup: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?

concept: The aircraft must have fully functioning dual controls for simulated instrument flight
q: What must the aircraft have installed for simulated instrument flight with a safety pilot?
a: Fully functioning dual controls. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.109, 'Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests.' The Warrior II has them as standard, so this is satisfied. The rule carries a narrow exception for certain aircraft equipped with a throwover control wheel, which has no application to a Piper Warrior.
dup: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?

concept: Safety pilot must have adequate visibility forward and to each side of the aircraft
q: What must a safety pilot be able to see?
a: The safety pilot must have adequate vision forward and to each side of the aircraft. Part 91, Subpart B, Flight Rules, 91.109. If the seating position or the airframe blocks that view, a competent observer carried aboard may supplement the safety pilot's vision. In a low wing Warrior II, check before the hood goes on that your safety pilot can actually see down and out on their side.
dup: What are the requirements for a safety pilot when logging simulated instrument time?

concept: An IPC is administered by a CFII, examiner, or FAA approved official
q: Who may administer an instrument proficiency check?
a: An examiner, an authorized instructor holding an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate, a company check pilot, a person authorized by the United States Armed Forces, or a person approved by the Administrator. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(d), 'Instrument proficiency check.' A flight instructor without the instrument rating on the certificate may not give one.
dup: Who may administer an instrument proficiency check?

concept: Some IPC tasks may be conducted in an Approved Aviation Training Device (AATD)
q: May part of an instrument proficiency check be conducted in a training device?
a: Yes. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(d) allows certain tasks in an approved flight simulator, flight training device, or advanced aviation training device, within the limits of the rule and the device's letter of authorization. The check follows the instrument rating areas of operation and tasks in the airman certification standards, and the remaining tasks are flown in the aircraft.

concept: Flight review required within the preceding 24 calendar months
q: How often must you complete a flight review?
a: Within the preceding 24 calendar months. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56, 'Flight review.' Without a current review you may not act as pilot in command of any aircraft, although you may still fly with an instructor. Calendar months means a review completed on 10 March 2025 is good through 31 March 2027. It is a currency requirement, not a certificate that expires.
dup: What is the flight review requirement, and what does the review consist of?

concept: Flight review includes a minimum of 1 hour of flight instruction
q: How much flight training must a flight review include?
a: A minimum of 1 hour of flight training. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56, 'Flight review.' The flight portion must review those maneuvers and procedures that, at the discretion of the instructor giving it, are necessary for you to exercise the privileges of your certificate safely. One hour is a floor, not a target; a rusty pilot should budget considerably more.
dup: What is the flight review requirement, and what does the review consist of?

concept: Flight review includes a minimum of 1 hour of ground instruction
q: How much ground training must a flight review include?
a: A minimum of 1 hour of ground training. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56, 'Flight review.' The ground portion must review the current general operating and flight rules of Part 91. There is no written test and no pass or fail entry in your logbook; the instructor either endorses the review as satisfactory or does not endorse it at all.
dup: What is the flight review requirement, and what does the review consist of?

concept: Flight review must be conducted by an authorized instructor
q: Who may conduct a flight review?
a: An authorized instructor, meaning a person holding a current flight instructor certificate with the appropriate ratings, or otherwise authorized by the Administrator to conduct it. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56, 'Flight review.' The instructor must be qualified in the category and class flown, and the review concludes with a logbook endorsement if it is satisfactory.
dup: What is the flight review requirement, and what does the review consist of?

concept: Flight review substitute: a proficiency check
q: Can a proficiency check substitute for a flight review?
a: Yes. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56(d) provides that a pilot who satisfactorily completes a pilot proficiency check conducted by the FAA, an approved pilot check airman, or the United States Armed Forces, for a pilot certificate, rating or operating privilege, need not accomplish the flight review. The check resets the 24 calendar month clock from the month it was completed.
dup: What can substitute for a flight review?

concept: Flight review substitute: a practical test for a new rating or certificate
q: Does passing a practical test count as a flight review?
a: Yes. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56(d): a satisfactory practical test for a new certificate, rating or operating privilege substitutes for the flight review. Passing your commercial pilot checkride therefore starts a fresh 24 calendar month period, which is why most commercial applicants do not need a separate review in the year they certificate.
dup: What can substitute for a flight review?

concept: Flight review substitute: completion of one or more phases of the WINGS pilot proficiency award program
q: How does the WINGS program substitute for a flight review?
a: Completing one or more phases of the FAA sponsored pilot proficiency award program, WINGS, within the preceding 24 calendar months satisfies the flight review requirement. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.56(e). A phase requires both knowledge credits earned online and flight activities flown with an instructor, all logged through the FAASafety.gov website.
dup: What can substitute for a flight review?

concept: Flight review substitute: flight instructor renewal under 61.197 substitutes for the ground portion only
q: A flight instructor renews their certificate. What does that do for the flight review?
a: It substitutes for the ground portion only. Part 61, Subpart H, 61.197, 'Renewal requirements for flight instructor certification,' read with 61.56(f): an instructor who satisfactorily completes a renewal of the flight instructor certificate need not accomplish the one hour of ground training. The one hour of flight training is still required to complete the review.
dup: What can substitute for a flight review?

concept: Passenger carrying day currency: 3 takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days
q: What must you have done to carry passengers by day?
a: Three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days, as the sole manipulator of the flight controls, in an aircraft of the same category, class and type if a type rating is required. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(a), 'Recent flight experience: Pilot in command.' For the Warrior II that means three in an airplane, single-engine land.
dup: What are the requirements to carry passengers by day in an airplane?

concept: The takeoffs and landings must be in the same aircraft category, class and type
q: For the 90 day passenger rule, what do category, class and type each mean?
a: Category is the broad grouping, such as airplane, rotorcraft or glider. Class is the subdivision within it, such as single-engine land, multiengine land or single-engine sea. Type is a specific make and model, and it only matters when the aircraft requires a type rating, generally above 12,500 pounds or turbojet powered. Three landings in any single-engine land airplane make you current for your Warrior II.
dup: For the 90-day passenger rule, what do category, class and type each mean?

concept: In a tailwheel airplane the day landings must be to a full stop
q: When must the three landings be to a full stop by day?
a: When the airplane is a tailwheel airplane. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(a)(2) requires the landings to be made to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane, because the handling risk in those aircraft is in the rollout. The Warrior II is a nosewheel airplane, so by day touch and goes count for it. At night all three must be full stop in any airplane.
dup: When must the three takeoffs and landings be to a full stop?

concept: Passenger carrying at night: 3 takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days, same category, class and type
q: What must you have done to carry passengers at night?
a: Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days, as sole manipulator of the controls, in an aircraft of the same category, class and type if a type rating is required, and performed during the defined night period. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(b), 'Night takeoff and landing experience.' Day currency does not carry over to night.
dup: What is required to carry passengers at night?

concept: Night passenger carrying landings must be to a full stop
q: Must night landings for passenger currency be to a full stop?
a: Yes, all three must be to a full stop, in every airplane, not merely in tailwheel types. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(b). A touch and go does not count at night. In practice that means taxiing back or flying a full pattern and stopping after each one, which is why night currency takes longer to accomplish in your Warrior II than day currency does.
dup: When must the three takeoffs and landings be to a full stop?

concept: Night for 61.57(b) is 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
q: What period counts as night for the 90 day night passenger currency rule?
a: From 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. Part 61, Subpart A, General, 61.57(b). Keep this apart from the other two definitions: night for logging night flight time under 61.51 is sunset to sunrise, and night for position and anti-collision lights under 91.209 is also sunset to sunrise. Only the currency rule uses the one hour buffer at each end.
dup: What are the three different definitions of night a commercial pilot must keep straight?

concept: These four ADS-B Out requirements are additional to the base requirement in Class A, B and C airspace
q: Why is this page headed Additional ADS-B Out requirements, and what is the base requirement?
a: Because ADS-B Out is first required in the busiest airspace: Class A, Class B and Class C. Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, 91.225, 'Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use.' The four items listed on this page extend that core requirement outward and upward into certain Class E airspace and the airspace around Class B and Class C.
dup: Where is ADS-B Out required?

concept: ADS-B Out in Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 ft AGL
q: Where is ADS-B Out required in Class E airspace over the continental United States?
a: At or above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL. The exclusion matters over high terrain: flying 2,000 feet above a 9,000 foot ridge puts you over 10,000 MSL but still inside the exclusion, so no ADS-B is required there. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.225, 'Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use.'
dup: Where is ADS-B Out required?

concept: ADS-B Out within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, the Mode C veil
q: Does the Mode C veil require ADS-B Out as well as a transponder?
a: Yes. Within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, both a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.215 and 91.225. The exception covers an aircraft not originally certificated with an engine driven electrical system; a 1981 Warrior II has one, so it needs the equipment.
dup: What is the Mode C veil and what does it require?

concept: ADS-B Out above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or C up to 10,000 ft MSL
q: Is ADS-B Out required above the ceiling of Class B or Class C airspace?
a: Yes, above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or Class C airspace, up to 10,000 feet MSL. Climbing over a Class C shelf at 5,500 feet to stay out of the airspace does not get you out of the equipment requirement. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.225, 'Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use.'
dup: Where is ADS-B Out required?

concept: ADS-B Out in Class E over the Gulf of Mexico at and above 3,000 ft MSL within 12 NM of the US coast
q: What is the ADS-B Out requirement over the Gulf of Mexico?
a: In Class E airspace over the Gulf of Mexico, at and above 3,000 feet MSL, within 12 nautical miles of the United States coast. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.225. The threshold is far lower than the 10,000 foot figure used over land because radar coverage offshore is poor and ADS-B is the primary means of surveillance in that airspace.
dup: Where is ADS-B Out required?

concept: No transponder installed: deviation request to the controlling ATC facility at least 1 hour before the proposed flight
q: Your airplane has no transponder and you want to fly through Class B. What must you do?
a: Submit a request for a deviation to the ATC facility having jurisdiction over the airspace, at least 1 hour before the proposed operation. Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, 91.215, 'ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use.' The request may be approved or denied, and you may not enter the airspace without the authorization.
dup: What is the exception to the transponder requirement, and how do you get a deviation?

concept: Transponder fails in flight in Class B: request immediately and a deviation may be issued to continue
q: Your transponder fails while you are inside Class B airspace. What do you do?
a: Tell ATC and request a deviation immediately. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.215 lets the controlling facility issue an authorization on the spot so you can continue through the airspace, and proceed to the airport of ultimate destination or to a place of repair. The one hour advance notice applies only to a planned flight in an aircraft with no transponder installed at all.
dup: What is the exception to the transponder requirement, and how do you get a deviation?

concept: Oxygen band: sea level up to and including 12,500 ft MSL, no supplemental oxygen required
q: Up to what cabin pressure altitude is no supplemental oxygen required at all?
a: Up to and including 12,500 feet MSL cabin pressure altitude, no supplemental oxygen is required, for any length of time and for anybody on board. Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' That band covers essentially all flying in a normally aspirated Warrior II, which cannot climb usefully much above it.

concept: Oxygen band: 12,501 ft to 14,000 ft MSL, required crew uses it for that part of the flight over 30 minutes
q: What is the oxygen requirement between 12,501 and 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude?
a: The minimum required flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes lasting more than 30 minutes. Part 91, Subpart C, Equipment, Instrument, and Certificate Requirements, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' A brief climb through the band needs nothing; a cruise segment longer than half an hour does. Nothing at all is required for passengers in this band.

concept: Oxygen band: above 14,000 ft MSL, flight crew must use oxygen at all times
q: What is the oxygen requirement above 14,000 feet cabin pressure altitude?
a: The minimum required flight crew must use supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes. There is no 30 minute grace period once you are above 14,000 feet MSL. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Passengers still need not be provided with oxygen until the cabin pressure altitude goes above 15,000 feet.

concept: Oxygen band: above 15,000 ft MSL, oxygen must be provided to every occupant
q: At what cabin pressure altitude must supplemental oxygen be provided to the passengers?
a: Above 15,000 feet MSL, each occupant of the aircraft must be provided with supplemental oxygen. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Note the wording precisely: provided, not used. Passengers are not required to use it, while the required flight crew has been required to use it continuously since 14,000 feet.

concept: Oxygen band: above 25,000 ft MSL, all lower requirements plus an additional 10 minutes of oxygen for each person on board
q: What extra oxygen must a pressurized aircraft carry above 25,000 feet?
a: Above flight level 250, on top of everything else 91.211 already requires, the aircraft must carry at least a 10 minute supplemental supply for each occupant, to cover the descent after a decompression. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Above flight level 350 one pilot at the controls must wear and use an oxygen mask, with a narrow quick donning exception below flight level 410.

concept: All the 91.211 MSL altitudes are cabin pressure altitudes, not aircraft altitudes
q: The oxygen altitudes in 91.211 are MSL altitudes of what, exactly?
a: Cabin pressure altitude, not the airplane's height above sea level. In an unpressurized airplane like the Warrior II the two are the same number, so the distinction never bites you. In a pressurized airplane cruising at flight level 250 with the cabin held at 8,000 feet, no oxygen is required, because cabin pressure altitude is what the rule measures.

concept: The exact breakpoints of the oxygen ladder: 12,500, 14,000, 15,000 and 25,000 ft MSL
q: State the four cabin pressure altitude breakpoints in the supplemental oxygen rule.
a: 12,500, 14,000, 15,000 and 25,000 feet MSL. Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 the crew uses it after 30 minutes; above 14,000 the crew uses it throughout; above 15,000 every occupant must be provided with it; above 25,000 a pressurized aircraft adds a 10 minute supply per occupant. Part 91, Subpart C, 91.211, 'Supplemental oxygen.' Each new band begins one foot above the stated figure.

concept: 91.21 general prohibition on portable electronic devices, and the two categories of flight it applies to
q: What does 91.21 prohibit, and on which flights does it actually apply?
a: It bars operating a portable electronic device aboard an aircraft, but only on two kinds of flight: an aircraft operated by the holder of an air carrier or operating certificate, and any other aircraft while it is being operated under IFR. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' A Part 91 VFR flight in your Warrior II falls outside the rule altogether.

concept: Electronic device exception 1: portable voice recorders
q: Name the first device 91.21 exempts from the portable electronic device prohibition.
a: Portable voice recorders. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' The exceptions exist because these devices either emit nothing capable of interfering with navigation and communication equipment, or are a necessity for the person using them. There are five exceptions in all: the first four are named outright and the fifth is a catch-all.

concept: Electronic device exception 2: hearing aids
q: Which hearing device is exempt from the 91.21 portable electronic device rule?
a: Hearing aids. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' Like the pacemaker exception, it is there because the device is a necessity for the person using it and because its emissions are negligible. No determination by the operator is needed for any of the four named items; only the fifth, catch-all category requires one.

concept: Electronic device exception 3: heart pacemakers
q: Which implanted medical device does 91.21 specifically exempt?
a: Heart pacemakers. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' It is third on the list of five exceptions, alongside portable voice recorders, hearing aids and electric shavers, with the fifth being anything else the operator has determined will not cause interference with navigation or communication systems.

concept: Electronic device exception 4: electric shavers
q: Which grooming device appears on the 91.21 exception list?
a: Electric shavers. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' It is the fourth of the five exceptions and the one applicants most often forget, which makes it a favorite oral exam question. In order the list reads portable voice recorders; hearing aids; heart pacemakers; electric shavers; and the operator determined catch-all.

concept: Electronic device exception 5: any other device the operator has determined will not cause interference with navigation or communication systems
q: What is the fifth, catch-all exception to the portable electronic device rule?
a: Any other portable electronic device that the operator of the aircraft has determined will not cause interference with the navigation or communication system of the aircraft in which it is to be used. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices.' This is the hook that lets tablets, portable GPS units, headsets and the like be used on an IFR flight.

concept: Who makes the no-interference determination under 91.21
q: Who makes the determination that a portable electronic device will not cause interference?
a: The operator of the aircraft. Part 91, Subpart A, General, 91.21, 'Portable electronic devices,' provides that for an aircraft operated by an air carrier or commercial operator the determination is made by that certificate holder, and for any other aircraft it is made by the pilot in command or other operator of the aircraft. Flying your Warrior II under IFR, that is you.

concept: Rime ice appearance: rough, milky, opaque ice
q: What does rime ice look like?
a: Rough, milky and opaque. The opacity comes from air trapped between the many small ice particles as the droplets freeze almost on contact. The roughness is the aerodynamic problem: it disrupts the airflow over the leading edge, raising drag, cutting lift, and lowering the angle of attack at which the wing stalls.
dup: What is rime ice and how does it form?

concept: Rime ice formation: instantaneous or very rapid freezing of supercooled droplets as they strike the leading edges
q: How does rime ice form?
a: By the instantaneous or very rapid freezing of small supercooled water droplets as they strike the leading edges. Because each droplet freezes where it hits, with no time to run back, rime builds forward into the airstream rather than spreading aft. It is typical of small droplets, colder temperatures and stratiform cloud, and is the kind a Warrior II most often picks up.
dup: What is rime ice and how does it form?

concept: Rime ice: rough surface decreases aerodynamic efficiency but it is lighter than clear ice
q: How does rime ice affect the airplane compared with clear ice?
a: The rough surface decreases aerodynamic efficiency, giving more drag, less lift and a lower stalling angle of attack, but rime is lighter than clear ice because it is full of trapped air. It is also brittle, so it sheds more readily from boots. Lighter does not mean harmless: in an unprotected airplane like the Warrior II, any accumulation means leave the icing conditions now.
dup: What is rime ice and how does it form?

concept: Clear ice: glossy, transparent ice formed by the relatively slow freezing of supercooled water
q: What is clear ice and how does it form?
a: Glossy, transparent ice formed by the relatively slow freezing of large supercooled water droplets. Because the droplets do not freeze on impact, they run back along the surface before freezing, spreading a smooth sheet over the airfoil. It is associated with large droplets, temperatures near freezing, cumuliform cloud and freezing rain.
dup: What is clear ice, how does it form, and why is it the worst kind?

concept: Clear ice is denser, harder, and sometimes more transparent than rime ice
q: How does clear ice compare with rime ice in density and hardness?
a: Clear ice is denser, harder and more transparent than rime. The density is what makes it dangerous: it adds real weight, and it can accumulate behind the protected part of a leading edge, altering the airfoil shape where no boot or heated surface can reach. It is also the type that builds fastest of all in freezing rain.
dup: What is clear ice, how does it form, and why is it the worst kind?

concept: Clear ice is harder to remove than rime ice
q: Which type of structural ice is harder to remove, and why?
a: Clear ice. It is dense, hard, and bonded tightly to the surface, so boots tend to crack it rather than shed it, and its runback formation leaves ice aft of the boot where nothing can reach. Rime is brittle and granular and comes off far more readily. In a Warrior II with no ice protection at all, the only answer to either type is to leave the conditions.
dup: What is clear ice, how does it form, and why is it the worst kind?

concept: Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime ice
q: What is mixed ice?
a: A combination of clear and rime ice, forming when supercooled droplets of widely differing sizes are present together, or when snow or ice particles become embedded in clear ice. The result is a rough, irregular, whitish accumulation with hard clear layers through it. It is common in cloud where droplet size varies through the layer.
dup: What is mixed ice?

concept: Mixed ice: roughness and weight can have an effect on aerodynamics
q: Why is mixed ice a problem aerodynamically?
a: Because it combines both penalties at once: the roughness of rime and the weight of clear ice. The irregular shape disrupts airflow, raising drag and stall speed, while the added mass cuts climb performance and useful load. It can also build into shapes that no deicing boot profile was designed to shed, leaving residual ice after a boot cycle.
dup: What is mixed ice?

concept: Airfoil cross-sections: the shape each of the three ice types makes on the leading edge
q: On the leading edge of a wing, how do the shapes of rime, clear and mixed ice differ?
a: Rime forms a thin, conformal cap that hugs the leading edge and builds forward into the airstream. Clear ice spreads as a smooth thin layer that runs back along the upper and lower surfaces well behind the leading edge. Mixed ice makes the bulkiest and most irregular shape, thickened at the leading edge with rough runback behind, which is why it distorts the airfoil the most.

concept: The four icing intensities, in order, are trace, light, moderate and severe
q: What are the four icing intensities used in pilot reports, from least to most severe?
a: Trace, light, moderate and severe. They are intensity categories, not thickness measurements: each is defined by what the accumulation does to the airplane and whether the ice protection equipment can cope with it. When you file a PIREP, give the intensity, the type, meaning rime, clear or mixed, and the altitude, the outside air temperature and the aircraft type.
dup: How are the four icing intensities defined for reporting?

concept: Trace icing definition: icing perceptible, not hazardous unless encountered for an extended period
q: How is trace icing defined?
a: Icing is perceptible, with the rate of accumulation slightly greater than the rate of loss through sublimation. It is not hazardous unless encountered for an extended period of time, generally taken as over an hour. Deicing or anti-icing equipment is not used unless the encounter lasts that long. In an unprotected Warrior II, even trace icing is a cue to change altitude.
dup: How are the four icing intensities defined for reporting?

concept: Light icing definition: icing clearly visible, anti-icing/deicing equipment removes or prevents accumulation
q: How is light icing defined?
a: Icing is clearly visible and accumulating, and it may present a problem if the flight continues in those conditions for more than an hour. Occasional use of deicing or anti-icing equipment removes or prevents the accumulation. In an airplane with no ice protection, light icing means exit the conditions immediately rather than wait out the hour.
dup: How are the four icing intensities defined for reporting?

concept: Moderate icing definition: even short encounters can be hazardous, equipment must be used or diversion required
q: How is moderate icing defined?
a: The rate of accumulation is such that even short encounters become potentially hazardous, so use of deicing or anti-icing equipment, or a diversion, is necessary. The definition turns on time: with moderate icing you no longer have an hour, you have minutes. Your Warrior II has no ice protection whatever, so for you the only available response is to divert.

concept: Severe icing definition: rate of accumulation is such that equipment fails to reduce the hazard, diversion mandatory
q: How is severe icing defined?
a: The rate of accumulation is such that deicing and anti-icing equipment fails to reduce or control the hazard, and immediate diversion is mandatory. Note that the definition rests on the equipment being overwhelmed, not on the thickness of the ice, so an airplane with no ice protection is not automatically in severe icing, though it also has no margin at all.
